description: Planetary Twin is an AI-powered platform that uses Earth observation data to identify and compare similar terrains on Earth, Mars, and the Moon. Using Machine Learning and satellite imagery, it matches geographical features and analyzes surface conditions. The Mission Test Lab provides an initial assessment of terrain suitability for rover movement, helping identify potential challenges and support future space exploration.
summary:
TerraTwin AI identifies Saudi Arabian landscapes that resemble selected regions on the Moon and Mars, helping users explore potential environments for early rover testing.

Our prototype compares elevation-derived terrain features, including slope, roughness, local relief, slope variability, and flat terrain. A transparent similarity engine identifies the closest match among the Saudi regions in our dataset based on three mission needs: mobility, navigation, and robotic operations.

Our Mission Test Lab takes this further by providing a preliminary assessment of easier and more challenging zones for rover movement based on slope and roughness. Users can explore both why an Earth region resembles the planetary target and which areas may be useful for testing.

By combining terrain matching, an interactive dashboard, and mission-focused assessment, TerraTwin AI connects planetary data with Saudi geography to support early testing discussions and educational exploration. It provides an initial screening tool, rather than certifying a location’s suitability or predicting actual rover performance.
details:
TerraTwin AI helps identify Saudi Arabian landscapes that resemble selected regions on the Moon and Mars. It combines terrain analysis, transparent similarity scoring, AI-assisted explanations, and a Mission Test Lab to support the early exploration of potential rover-testing environments.

How it works

Our prototype compares AlUla and Harrat Khaybar in Saudi Arabia with Connecting Ridge on the Moon and Athabasca Valles on Mars. We process digital elevation models in QGIS and compare five terrain characteristics: mean slope, roughness, local relief, slope variability, and flat fraction. Our study areas cover approximately 16 × 16 km and are processed at a common 75 m resolution.

Users select a planetary target and a mission condition, or describe their needs in natural language. The system supports three comparison conditions:

• Mobility uses slope, roughness, local relief, and slope variability.
• Navigation uses roughness, local relief, and slope variability.
• Robotic Operations uses slope, roughness, and flat fraction.

The similarity engine calculates the absolute difference between each Earth and planetary feature value, normalizes it by the feature’s reference range, and averages the differences using equal weights. It converts this distance into a similarity percentage and identifies the closest Saudi candidate.

AI assists with interpreting user requests and explaining the computed results. The numerical similarity scores come from the mathematical engine, not from a language model.

Mission Test Lab

Mission Test Lab takes the project beyond finding a similar landscape. It presents precomputed proportions of Low, Medium, and High terrain difficulty for the Earth candidate and planetary target, using a hybrid classification based on slope thresholds and roughness percentiles.

Low difficulty requires slope below 10° and roughness below 31.28 m. High difficulty indicates slope of at least 15° or roughness of at least 68.30 m. Remaining valid terrain cells are classified as Medium.

This helps users understand that terrain similarity and movement difficulty are separate questions. A location can resemble a planetary region while still containing challenging terrain. The lab supports preliminary testing discussions; it does not simulate rover physics or certify safe routes.

Benefits and intended impact

TerraTwin AI helps students, researchers, and robotics teams explore potential terrestrial analogues and understand the measurable reasons behind a match. By highlighting Saudi landscapes, it encourages local engagement with planetary science and supports more informed planning before detailed field investigations.

Tools and resources

We use Python, Pandas, and NumPy for data processing and similarity calculations, QGIS for geospatial analysis, and Streamlit for the dashboard. JSON and CSV outputs connect the analysis components. Groq-hosted language models support mission interpretation and result explanations, with deterministic fallback explanations when the API is unavailable.

Our elevation sources include SRTM for Earth, NASA LRO LOLA for the Moon, and ESA Mars Express HRSC for Mars.

Creativity and design considerations

The project combines mission-specific terrain matching with a separate terrain difficulty assessment in one workflow. Users can explore both why a region was selected and what terrain challenges it contains.

We considered differences in source resolution, consistent feature definitions, explainable scoring, API availability, and the distinction between resemblance and operational suitability. Processing datasets at a common resolution does not make their original accuracy or detail identical.

The prototype has a limited candidate dataset and does not account for gravity, temperature, radiation, soil strength, or rover design. Equal feature weights and difficulty thresholds require further validation. Results are intended for preliminary screening and educational exploration, with field measurements and expert review required before operational use.
